title: Transport and communication: how people, goods and messages travel

summary.text: The rice in your kitchen may have come hundreds of kilometres by truck or train. A phone call reaches Ammamma in Mysuru in less than a second. Transport is how people and goods move from place to place: by road, rail, water, air and pipeline. Communication is how messages and ideas travel: by speech, signs, letters, phones, radio, TV and the internet. In this unit you follow how both grew, from footpaths and boats to metros and satellites. You learn what road signs and traffic lights mean, and how transport dirties the air. Then you test, in a dark room, which clothes a driver can see from furthest away.
summary.art: A busy Indian street at dusk seen from a balcony: a bus, an auto, a cyclist and a walker, a red-circle road sign and a traffic light, with a phone tower and a satellite in the evening sky above.

intro.hook: Pick up one packet from your kitchen shelf, such as rice, salt or tea. Read where it was packed. Who carried it to your home, and how?
intro.text: Almost nothing in your home was made in your home. Salt may come from Thoothukudi or Gujarat. Tea may come from the Nilgiris or Assam. It came by truck, train or ship, and then by a shop's van or a delivery scooter. People also need to send messages: to order the rice, to pay for it, to say 'it has arrived'. In this unit you find out how people learned to carry things and messages further and faster. You also find out how roads keep people safe, and test whether a driver can really see you at night.
intro.art: A child at a kitchen shelf holding a packet of rice, with a dotted line from the packet out of the window to a truck, a train and a map of India.

outcomes: By the end I can tell how transport grew, from walking and boats to wheels, trains, ships and aeroplanes.
By the end I can name the kinds of transport (road, rail, water, air and pipeline) and say what each is best for.
By the end I can explain how communication grew, and tell one-way communication from two-way communication.
By the end I can read common road signs and traffic lights, and say what their shapes and colours mean.
By the end I can explain, using my dark-room test, why white clothes and reflective strips keep a walker safe at night.
By the end I can say how transport harms the air and our health, and choose ways to travel that pollute less.

terms.meaning: Transport means moving people or goods from one place to another. It can be by road, rail, water, air or pipeline.
terms.example: A train carrying rice from Andhra Pradesh to Kerala is transport. So is your walk to the shop.
terms.art: A truck, a train, a boat and an aeroplane in a row, each carrying sacks.

terms.meaning: Communication means sharing messages, feelings and ideas with others. It can be by talking, signs, writing, phones, radio, TV or the internet.
terms.example: Waving goodbye, writing a letter and making a video call are all communication.
terms.art: A girl waving from a balcony and her grandmother waving back from a phone screen.

terms.meaning: A vehicle is a machine that carries people or goods, such as a bus, a cycle, an auto, a boat or an aeroplane.
terms.example: An auto-rickshaw is a three-wheeled vehicle.
terms.art: A yellow-and-green auto-rickshaw with a driver.

terms.meaning: A wheel is a round frame that turns. The axle is the rod at its centre that the wheel turns around. Together they let a heavy load roll instead of being dragged.
terms.example: A bullock cart has two big wooden wheels joined by one axle.
terms.art: A bullock cart wheel with the axle rod through its centre, an arrow showing it turning.

terms.meaning: A pipeline is a long pipe that carries a liquid or a gas over a long distance, such as water, petrol or cooking gas.
terms.example: In some cities, cooking gas comes to the kitchen through a pipe, not in a cylinder.
terms.art: A long pipe on stands crossing fields towards a city.

terms.meaning: A traffic signal is a set of lights that tells vehicles when to stop and go. Red means stop. Amber means get ready to stop. Green means go.
terms.example: At a busy junction in Hyderabad, cars stop at the red light.
terms.art: A traffic signal with red, amber and green lights, the red one lit.

terms.meaning: A road sign is a board by the road that gives a message with a shape, a colour and a picture. Most road signs use no words, so anyone can understand them.
terms.example: A red circle with a crossed-out horn means 'Do not sound your horn here'.
terms.art: A round road sign with a red border and a crossed-out horn, near a hospital gate.

terms.meaning: A zebra crossing is a set of wide white stripes painted across a road. It shows where people on foot may cross, and vehicles must stop for them.
terms.example: Children cross at the zebra crossing outside a school in Madurai.
terms.art: White stripes across a road with a child and a grown-up crossing hand in hand.

terms.meaning: To reflect is to send light back. Light from a lamp hits a thing, and some of it bounces off. We see the thing when that light reaches our eyes. A white cloth reflects much more light than a black cloth.
terms.example: A white shirt reflects a lot of a car's headlight. A black shirt reflects very little.
terms.art: A torch beam hitting a white cloth and a black cloth, with many arrows bouncing back from the white one and few from the black one.

terms.meaning: A reflective strip is a shiny band that sends light straight back towards the lamp it came from. It shines brightly to the driver whose headlights hit it.
terms.example: Many school bags, helmets and cycle pedals have reflective strips.
terms.art: A school bag with a silver strip glowing in a car's headlight.

terms.meaning: In one-way communication, the message goes from the sender to the receiver, and the receiver cannot answer back straight away.
terms.example: A radio programme, a road sign and a newspaper are one-way.
terms.art: A radio on a shelf playing, with a child listening, and an arrow going only from the radio to the child.

terms.meaning: In two-way communication, both people can send and receive messages, so the listener can ask questions.
terms.example: A phone call and a talk at the dinner table are two-way.
terms.art: Two children talking on toy phones, with arrows going both ways.

terms.meaning: Mass communication sends one message to a very large number of people at once.
terms.example: A cricket match on TV reaches millions of homes at the same time.
terms.art: A TV tower sending lines out to many houses.

terms.meaning: A satellite is something that goes round the Earth again and again. People send machines up into space to be satellites. Communication satellites pass on phone, TV and internet signals.
terms.example: Your TV dish points up at a satellite far above the Earth.
terms.art: A satellite with solar panels above the Earth, and a dish on an Indian rooftop pointing at it.

terms.meaning: A PIN code is the 6-digit number in an Indian address. PIN stands for Postal Index Number. It tells the post office which area a letter must go to.
terms.example: The PIN code 600001 is for an area in Chennai.
terms.art: An envelope with an address and six boxes at the bottom for the PIN code.

terms.meaning: Pollution is anything harmful that we add to air, water or land. Vehicle smoke and loud horns are two kinds of pollution.
terms.example: A bus with an old engine leaves a cloud of black smoke behind.
terms.art: A road with black smoke coming out of an old truck, and a child covering her nose.

terms.meaning: Exhaust is the smoke and gas that come out of a vehicle's engine when it burns petrol or diesel. It has carbon dioxide and tiny specks of soot in it.
terms.example: You can smell the exhaust behind a bus at a bus stop.
terms.art: The exhaust pipe at the back of a scooter with grey gas coming out.

explanations.concept: Why a dark shirt is hard to see at night
explanations.definition: We see a thing only when light from it reaches our eyes. At night, a driver sees a walker only by the headlight that bounces off the walker and comes back. White and pale colours reflect much more light than black and dark colours.
explanations.description: In the dark-room test, the same dim torch shone on every cloth. The black cloth vanished a few steps away, because it reflected very little of the light. The white cloth reflected most of the light, so it stayed visible much further away. A reflective strip is special. It sends light straight back towards the lamp, so it shines brightly to the person holding the torch, or the driver behind the headlights. A driver going fast needs to see a walker from far away, to have time to slow down. So at night, walkers should wear pale clothes and something reflective, and carry a torch.
examples: A walker in a white mundu or a white school shirt is seen from much further away than one in a black shirt.
A cycle's red back reflector shines brightly in a car's headlight, though it has no battery.
Traffic police at night wear jackets with reflective stripes.
explanations.art: A dark road at night with a car's headlights shining on two walkers: one in white, clearly lit, and one in black, almost invisible.
explanations.context: This card explains what the dark-room test showed: why a driver can see some clothes from much further away than others.

explanations.definition: Transport grew from walking and carrying, to boats on rivers, to animals and carts with wheels, to engines that burn coal, petrol or diesel, and to electric trains and aeroplanes.
explanations.description: The first transport was walking. People carried loads on their heads and backs, and made footpaths by walking the same way again and again. Boats are older than wheels. A wooden canoe found in the Netherlands is about 10,000 years old. The wheel was invented about 5,500 years ago. Clay toy carts with wheels, about 4,500 years old, have been found at Harappa and Mohenjo-daro. Animals pulled carts for thousands of years. Then steam engines came, and India's first passenger train ran from Bombay to Thane in 1853. Cars, buses, aeroplanes and metros followed. Each change carried more people and goods, faster and further.
examples: The first passenger train in South India ran from Royapuram in Madras in 1856.
Kattumaram, the Tamil name for a raft of logs tied together, gave English the word 'catamaran'.
Kochi started India's first water metro, with electric boats, in 2023.
explanations.art: A time-line strip from left to right: a person carrying a basket on a footpath, a log boat, a bullock cart, a steam train, a bus, an aeroplane and a metro train.
explanations.context: This card tells the story of how people learned to move themselves and their goods further and faster.

explanations.definition: There are five main kinds of transport: road, rail, water, air and pipeline. Each is best for different journeys.
explanations.description: Road transport, such as cycles, autos, buses and trucks, goes almost everywhere, right up to the door. Rail transport carries many people and heavy goods a long way, cheaply, but only where there are tracks. Water transport by boats and ships is the cheapest way to carry very heavy goods across seas and along rivers, but it is slow. Air transport is the fastest over long distances, but it costs the most and uses a lot of fuel. Pipelines carry water, petrol and gas without any vehicle at all. Most goods travel by more than one kind. Rice may go by train to a city, then by truck to a shop.
examples: A fisherwoman in Kollam takes her fish to the market in an auto: road transport.
Coal reaches power stations in long goods trains: rail transport.
Big ships carry cars and machines into Chennai port: water transport.
explanations.art: Five panels: a truck on a ghat road, a goods train, a cargo ship at a port, an aeroplane, and a pipeline crossing a field.
explanations.context: This card names the five kinds of transport and what each one is best at.

explanations.definition: Communication grew from gestures and speech, to drums, smoke and messengers, to writing and the post, and then to electric messages: the telegraph, the telephone, radio, TV and the internet.
explanations.description: People first shared messages face to face, with sounds, faces and hand movements. To reach further, they beat drums, lit fires and sent runners and pigeons. Writing let a message travel without the person who wrote it. India's postal department began in 1854. The telegraph sent messages as short and long pulses of electricity along wires. Telephones carried the voice itself. Radio and TV sent sounds and pictures through the air to millions of homes. India's last telegram was sent in 2013. Today a phone sends messages as radio waves to a tower, and from there through cables or satellites to almost anywhere in the world in under a second.
examples: The Radio Club of Madras began radio broadcasts in Chennai in 1924.
Odisha police kept a pigeon post service running until 2008.
PIN codes began in India on 15 August 1972.
explanations.art: A time-line strip: a person waving, a drum, a pigeon with a note, a letter and post box, a telegraph key, an old telephone, a radio, a TV and a mobile phone.
explanations.context: This card tells the story of how people learned to send messages further and faster.

explanations.definition: In one-way communication, the receiver cannot answer back straight away. In two-way communication, both sides can send and receive, so the listener can ask questions.
explanations.description: A road sign, a radio programme and a newspaper are one-way. They can reach very many people at once. But if the message is unclear, nobody can ask what it meant. A phone call or a talk is two-way. The listener can say, 'Do you mean the big circle or the small one?' Two-way talk usually gets the message across more correctly, but it takes longer. This is why road signs must be very simple. A driver going past at speed cannot ask the sign a question.
examples: A teacher on a video lesson cannot hear your question. A teacher in the room can.
A letter is two-way, but slow: the answer may take a week.
A WhatsApp message is two-way, but the reply may come late.
explanations.art: On the left, a radio sending arrows one way to a listener. On the right, two children on phones with arrows going both ways.
explanations.context: This card explains the difference you tested in the Words Only test: one-way and two-way messages.

explanations.definition: Road signs give their message by shape and colour, so they can be read from far away and without words. In India, a circle gives an order, a triangle gives a warning, and a rectangle gives information.
explanations.description: A red circle says what you must not do, such as 'No horn' or 'No entry'. A blue circle says what you must do, such as 'Go straight only'. A triangle with a red border warns you of something ahead, such as a school, a speed breaker or a sharp bend. A blue rectangle gives information, such as the way to a hospital or a petrol pump. The STOP sign is a red eight-sided shape. Traffic lights use red for stop, amber for get ready to stop, and green for go. People on foot have their own lights: a red standing person and a green walking person. These rules let thousands of strangers share a road without crashing into each other.
examples: A triangle with two children on it means 'School ahead: slow down'.
A red circle with '40' inside means 'Do not go faster than 40 kilometres an hour'.
A blue rectangle with a fuel pump picture means 'Petrol pump this way'.
explanations.art: Three road signs side by side: a red-bordered circle with a crossed-out horn, a red-bordered triangle with two children, and a blue rectangle with a fuel pump.
explanations.context: This card explains how to read a road sign by its shape and colour, even before you see the picture.

explanations.concept: How transport affects the air and our health
explanations.definition: Vehicles that burn petrol or diesel give out exhaust. Exhaust has carbon dioxide, which warms the Earth, and tiny specks of soot and harmful gases, which hurt our lungs. Horns and engines also cause noise pollution.
explanations.description: In big cities, much of the dirty air comes from vehicles. Breathing it for years can make people ill, especially children and old people. Carbon dioxide from engines adds to the gases that are warming the whole Earth. Walking and cycling make no exhaust at all. A full bus or metro carries many people with much less fuel for each person than if they all drove. Electric vehicles give out no exhaust on the road, but their electricity often comes from power stations that burn coal. So the cleanest journey is often the one we walk, cycle or share.
examples: A Chennai Metro train carries hundreds of people at once on electricity.
A cycle ride to the shop makes no smoke and no noise.
Some hospital and school zones have 'No horn' signs to cut noise.
explanations.art: A road split in two: on one side a traffic jam with smoke, on the other a metro train, cyclists and walkers under trees.
explanations.context: This card explains how the way we travel changes the air we breathe.

explanations.concept: How a radio message gets past the curve of the Earth
explanations.definition: Some radio waves bounce off a layer of charged air high above the Earth, called the ionosphere. This lets them reach places far beyond the horizon. Today, satellites also pass on signals across the world.
explanations.description: Radio waves travel in straight lines, like light. The Earth is round, so a straight line soon leaves the ground and heads into space. In 1901, Guglielmo Marconi reported a radio signal sent across the Atlantic Ocean, much further than straight lines should allow. Later, scientists showed that a layer high in the air, the ionosphere, sends some radio waves back down. Now communication satellites go round the Earth high above us. They catch signals from one place and send them down to another, far away.
examples: Short-wave radio from other countries can be heard at night in India because of the ionosphere.
A live cricket match in Australia reaches TVs in India through satellites and undersea cables.
India's INSAT satellites pass on TV and weather signals.
explanations.art: The curved Earth with a radio tower on one side, a zigzag path of radio waves bouncing between the ground and a glowing layer high in the sky, and a satellite further out.
explanations.context: This card explains how radio messages reach places beyond the curve of the Earth.

explanations.concept: How other living beings send messages
explanations.description: People are not the only beings who communicate. A honeybee who finds flowers comes back and dances on the comb. The direction of her dance tells the other bees which way to fly, and its length tells them how far. Ants leave a trail of smell from food to the nest, and others follow it. Crows give loud calls when they see a cat or a snake, and other crows gather. Plants send messages too. When insects chew a plant's leaves, the plant releases smells into the air, and nearby plants make their own defences ready.
examples: Put a grain of sugar near an ant line and watch others come along the same path.
A crow cawing loudly at a cat on the wall brings other crows.
Freshly cut grass smells strong: those smells are messages the grass sends.

perspectives.explanation: A plant senses an attack and sends out smells that warn their neighbours, who get ready. That is communication, like a crow's warning call.
The smells may be meant for the plant's own other leaves, or for insects that eat the attackers. The neighbours may simply be 'overhearing'. They prefer the word 'signalling'.

explanations.art: A honeybee dancing on a comb with other bees around her, an ant trail to a sugar grain, and a tomato plant with faint smell lines reaching a neighbour plant.
explanations.context: This card is about how bees, ants, crows and plants share messages without words.

agreed.text: At night, drivers see pale clothes and reflective strips from much further away than dark clothes.
agreed.evidence: You can test it with a dim torch in a dark room. Road safety studies with real drivers find the same.

agreed.text: Boats are much older than wheels.
agreed.evidence: Log canoes about 10,000 years old have been dug up. The oldest wheels found are about 5,500 years old.

agreed.text: Vehicle exhaust makes city air unhealthy and adds carbon dioxide, which warms the Earth.
agreed.evidence: Air-quality stations in Indian cities measure soot and gases near roads, and doctors find more lung illness where the air is dirtiest.

agreed.text: Two-way communication usually gets a message across more correctly than one-way communication, but it takes longer.
agreed.evidence: Studies since the 1950s have tested this with people describing shapes, just like the Words Only test.

agreed.text: Some radio waves are bent back to the ground by the ionosphere, a charged layer high in the air.
agreed.evidence: Edward Appleton measured radio echoes from this layer in 1924, and radio stations use it every day.

challenging.claim: People travelled on wheels before they travelled in boats.
challenging.for: The wheel is often called the greatest invention, so many people think it came first.
challenging.against: Log canoes about 10,000 years old have been found. The oldest wheels are about 5,500 years old. People also crossed the sea to reach Australia more than 50,000 years ago, so they must have had boats or rafts.
challenging.context: This card is about which came first, the boat or the wheel.

challenging.claim: Bright neon colours, like fluorescent green or orange, keep you safe at night.
challenging.for: Fluorescent colours look very bright in the daytime and at dusk.
challenging.against: Fluorescent colours glow using some of the invisible light in sunlight. Most headlights give out almost none of it. At night a fluorescent jacket is seen about as well as a plain pale one. Reflective strips work far better.
challenging.context: This card is about which clothes keep a walker safe in the dark.

challenging.for: Marconi built the first radio system that worked over long distances and sold it to ships and governments. He shared the Nobel Prize in 1909.
challenging.against: Many people worked on radio at the same time. In Kolkata in the 1890s, J.C. Bose made and detected very short radio waves. Nikola Tesla, Alexander Popov and others also built radio devices. Most historians say radio had many inventors.
challenging.context: This card is about who should get the credit for radio.

challenging.claim: Electric scooters and cars cause no pollution.
challenging.for: They give out no exhaust on the road, so the air on the street is cleaner.
challenging.against: Their electricity is often made by burning coal in power stations. Making their batteries uses a lot of energy. Their tyres and brakes still make dust.
challenging.context: This card is about whether electric vehicles are really clean.

challenging.claim: If I can see the car, the driver can see me.
challenging.who: A common belief, among children and grown-ups
challenging.for: The car's headlights look very bright to you.
challenging.against: You see the bright lamp itself. The driver sees you only by the little light that bounces off you. In the dark-room test, the black cloth vanished a few steps away while the torch was still shining.
challenging.context: This card is about a mistake that causes many night-time accidents.

big_questions.q: When you see a friend across the room, does anything go from you to your friend, or only from your friend to you?
big_questions.hint: Think of the dark-room test. Where did the light start, where did it bounce, and where did it end?

big_questions.q: If someone sends a message and nobody receives it, has anything been communicated?
big_questions.hint: Think of a letter that gets lost in the post, or a road sign that nobody passes.

big_questions.q: A whisper changes as it is passed along a line of people. A written note does not. Why?
big_questions.hint: In the Words Only test, what went wrong when the listener could not ask?

big_questions.q: Bees dance, ants leave smells and plants release smells. What counts as a language?
big_questions.hint: Does a language need words? Does it need a mouth?

big_questions.q: Your great-grandparents may never have gone more than a day's walk from home. Is it better that we travel so much more?
big_questions.hint: Think of what fast travel gives us, and what it costs the air and the Earth.

big_questions.q: Roads and phones join faraway people. Do they make people feel closer, or further apart?
big_questions.hint: Think of a video call with a grandparent, and a family all looking at different phones at dinner.

story.title: Paati's Night Bus
story.note: Women drive buses in Kerala today. Saraswathi, Kavya, Arjun and this evening in Kochi are made up. Reflective strips, cycle reflectors and road signs work exactly as the story says.
text: Kavya was nine, and her cousin Arjun was six. Every summer they stayed with their grandmother, Saraswathi Paati, in a small flat in Kochi. Paati had driven buses for thirty years. She had driven up the ghat roads to Munnar, and through the night to Thrissur.
One evening the power went off. The lane outside was dark, except for the lights of passing autos. Arjun pulled on his black T-shirt. 'I will run across to the shop and buy the milk,' he said.
'Wait,' said Paati. 'First come to the balcony. I want to show you something.'

The three of them stood at the rail and looked down at the lane. An auto came round the corner, its one headlight shining ahead. In front of it walked a man in a white mundu. Kavya saw him clearly, long before the auto reached him.
'There is someone else down there too,' said Paati quietly. 'Can you see him?'

Kavya looked and looked. She saw nothing. Then the auto came close, and suddenly there was a boy in a dark blue shirt, right in front of it. The driver honked and swerved. The boy jumped to the side. Arjun gasped.
'He was there the whole time,' said Paati. 'The driver could not see him until the very last moment.'
'But the headlight was so bright,' said Arjun. 'I could see it from up here.'

'You could see the lamp,' said Paati. 'That is different from the driver seeing the boy. The driver sees him only by the light that bounces off him and comes back. A white mundu sends back a lot of light. A dark shirt sends back very little.'
Next came a girl on a cycle. Her cycle had no lamp. But as the next auto came up behind her, a red spot on the back of her cycle flashed brightly.
'Her reflector,' said Kavya. 'It has no battery. How does it shine?'
Paati went inside and came back with a torch and Kavya's school bag. She held the torch right next to her own eye and pointed it at the bag across the balcony. A grey strip on the bag blazed silver.

'Now you hold the bag, and I will stand to the side,' said Paati. She asked Kavya to point the torch at the bag again. From where Paati stood, the strip looked dull. From where Kavya held the torch, it shone.
'This strip sends light straight back to wherever it came from,' said Paati. 'So it shines brightest for the person holding the lamp. On the road, that person is the driver.'
'Like the road signs on the ghat road,' said Kavya. 'They light up in the headlights.'

'Yes,' said Paati. 'When I drove the night bus to Munnar, nobody had switched on those signs. The bend signs and the speed breaker signs glowed only when my own headlights hit them. They were made to send my light back to me. A road sign is a message. It cannot shout. It can only send back the light that falls on it.'
Arjun looked down at his black T-shirt. Then he went inside and came back in his white school shirt.
'Better,' said Paati. She gave him the torch. 'Carry this, and shine it down at the road in front of you. Then the driver will see your light. You will see the road too.'
Kavya went with him, holding his hand. At the edge of the lane they stopped, looked right, then left, then right again. An auto was coming. They waited until it passed. Then they crossed.
When they came back with the milk, Arjun was thinking hard. 'Paati,' he said, 'when I see you, does anything go from my eyes to you?'
Paati laughed. 'Now that is a question even I never asked on the night bus. What do you think?'
story.epiphany: For the parent: a driver sees a walker only by the headlight that bounces off the walker and returns to the driver's eyes. A white mundu reflects much of that light, so the man was seen from far away. The dark blue shirt reflected very little, so the boy was seen only when the auto was very close. Seeing the bright lamp does not mean the driver can see you. A reflector, like the red one on a cycle or the strip on a school bag, sends light straight back towards its source, so it shines brightly for the driver and much less for someone standing to the side. Many road signs are covered with the same kind of sheeting. Arjun's last question has a plain answer: nothing goes out from our eyes to make us see. We see when light comes into them.
ask: Why could Kavya see the man in the white mundu long before the auto reached him?
Arjun could see the auto's headlight from the balcony. Why did that not mean the driver could see the boy?
Why did the strip on the bag shine for Kavya, who held the torch, but not for Paati, standing to the side?
What three things did Arjun do to be safe when he crossed the lane?
Paati says a road sign 'can only send back the light that falls on it'. What did she mean?

rules: Shuffle the cards and put them face down.
Turn over the top card and read the front aloud.
First say what kind of sign it is from its shape: circle (an order), triangle (a warning) or rectangle (information). That is 1 point.
Then say what it means. Check the back. A right meaning is 1 more point.
Playing alone, try to beat your own score. With others, take turns.
The first player to 15 points wins.

flow.context: This is the first step of Sign Snap. You set up the cards.
flow.do: 1. Cut out the 20 cards. 2. Shuffle them and put them face down. 3. Read the rules aloud.
flow.say: In this game, the shape of a sign tells you its kind before you even see the picture. Circles give orders, triangles warn, and rectangles give information.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Mix them up. Put them face down. Circles give orders. Triangles warn. Rectangles give information.

flow.do: 1. Take turns: turn a card, read the front, name the kind of sign, then say its meaning. 2. Check the back and score.
flow.say: What shape is it? So what kind of sign is it? Now, what does it tell the driver or the walker to do?
flow.kid: Turn a card. Say its shape and its kind. Then say what it means. Check the back.

ask.q: Why do you think warning signs and order signs have different shapes?
good: So a driver knows the kind of sign from far away.
So you know before you can see the picture.

flow.do: Count the points and talk about which signs were hardest.
flow.say: Which sign was hardest? Why do you think road signs use pictures, not words?
flow.kid: Count your points. Which sign was hardest? Why do signs use pictures, not words?

check.q: A sign is a circle with a red border. What kind of sign is it?
options: An order saying what you must not do
A sign for a zebra crossing
check.why: In India, a circle gives an order. A red circle says what you must not do, such as 'No horn' or 'No entry'. Triangles warn, and blue rectangles give information.

setup.art: Nineteen small cut-out cards on a table, showing red circles, red-bordered triangles, blue circles and blue rectangles.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the sign cards and put them face down.

setup.art: A girl turning over a card with a red-bordered triangle and two children, saying 'Triangle: a warning!'
setup.caption: 2. Turn a card. Name its shape and kind, then its meaning.

games.title: Send It! Choose the best way to carry it
games.context: This is a card game about choosing transport and communication. You get a job, choose a way to do it, and argue why your choice is best.

items.f: Wish Ammamma in Mysuru a happy birthday today.
items.b: A phone or video call: fast and two-way. A posted card would arrive late.

items.f: Carry 1,000 sacks of rice from Andhra Pradesh to Kerala.
items.b: A goods train: carries heavy loads a long way cheaply.

items.f: Take a sick person to hospital, 5 kilometres away, quickly.
items.b: An ambulance: fast, and other vehicles must give way to it.

items.f: Tell everyone in Tamil Nadu that a cyclone is coming.
items.b: Radio, TV and phone alerts: mass communication reaches millions at once.

items.f: Send 2,000 new cars from Chennai to another country.
items.b: A big ship: the cheapest way to carry very heavy goods across the sea.

items.f: Get from Kochi to Delhi by tomorrow morning.
items.b: An aeroplane: the fastest over long distances, though it uses a lot of fuel.

items.f: Buy milk from the shop at the end of your lane.
items.b: Walk: no smoke, no noise and no cost.

items.f: Bring cooking gas to every flat in a big building.
items.b: A gas pipeline, or cylinders brought by a delivery van.

items.f: Warn a driver that a school is just ahead.
items.b: A road sign: a red-bordered triangle with two children.

items.f: Tell a friend who is deaf, across a noisy room, that it is time to go.
items.b: A gesture or sign language: no sound needed.

items.f: Get 300 people to their offices in a crowded city.
items.b: A metro or buses: many people, much less smoke for each person.

items.f: Send a photo to a cousin in Kolkata right now.
items.b: The internet, by phone: it arrives in seconds.

rules: Shuffle the job cards and put them face down. Spread the means cards face up.
Turn over a job card and read it aloud.
Each player picks the means card they think is best and says why.
Read the back of the job card. A choice that matches gets 2 points.
A different choice with a good reason gets 1 point, if the other players agree.
After all 12 jobs, the player with most points wins.

flow.context: This is the first step of Send It! You set up the job cards and the means cards.
flow.do: 1. Cut out both sets of cards. 2. Put the job cards face down. 3. Spread the means cards face up.
flow.say: Every job needs a way to carry something, or a way to send a message. You choose the best way, and give your reason.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Put the job cards face down. Spread the means cards face up.

flow.do: 1. Turn a job card and read it. 2. Each player picks a means card and gives a reason. 3. Read the back and score.
flow.say: Which way is best for this job? Think about how fast, how much it can carry, how much it costs and how much smoke it makes.
flow.kid: Read the job. Pick the best way. Say why. Check the back.

ask.q: Why is a goods train better than trucks for 1,000 sacks of rice?
good: One train carries the load of many trucks.
It uses less fuel for each sack.
It is cheaper over a long way.

flow.do: Count points, and talk about a job where two answers were both good.
flow.say: Was there a job where two different choices were both good? What made them good?
flow.kid: Count your points. Which job had two good answers?

check.q: Which is the cheapest way to carry 2,000 cars across the sea?
check.why: Ships carry very heavy loads across the sea more cheaply than any other way. Aeroplanes are faster but cost far more. Trucks and pipelines cannot cross the sea.

setup.art: Job cards face down in a pile and twelve means cards spread out face up: walking, cycle, auto, bus, metro, goods train, ship, aeroplane, pipeline, phone call, radio and TV, road sign.
setup.caption: 1. Put the job cards face down. Spread the means cards face up.

setup.art: A mother and son each holding up a means card, a goods train and a truck, with a job card about 1,000 sacks of rice between them.
setup.caption: 2. Read a job. Each player picks a way and says why.

experiments.title: Seen in the Dark: which clothes can a driver see from furthest away?
experiments.context: In this experiment you are a driver at night. In a dark room, you shine a dim torch at different cloths and find how far away you can still see each one.
experiments.question: At night, how far away can a driver see a black cloth, a dark cloth, a white cloth and a yellow cloth?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Which cloth will you still see from furthest away? Which one will vanish first? How many foot-steps away do you think each will vanish? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same torch, covered the same way, for every cloth. Hang every cloth on the same chair in the same place, with the same dark room behind it. Keep the room just as dark each time. The same person looks every time, holding the torch next to their eye like a car's headlight. Only the cloth changes. Test each cloth twice, because one try can be a fluke.

materials.item: a black cloth about the size of a T-shirt: a black T-shirt, dupatta or towel
a dark cloth in another colour: dark blue, dark brown or dark green
a white cloth of the same size: a white shirt, towel or vesti
a yellow or orange cloth, if you have one
a torch, or a phone with a torch
a white handkerchief and a rubber band, to make the torch dim
a chair
optional: a school bag, shoe, helmet or cycle with a reflective strip or reflector, and a piece of kitchen foil

experiments.safety: A grown-up stays in the room the whole time. Clear the floor before switching off the lights, because the child walks backwards in the dark. Walk slowly, heel to toe. Never shine the torch into anyone's eyes.

schedule.what: Set up the chair in a doorway. Guess. Test each cloth twice in the dark with a dim torch. Then try a reflective strip.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw a bar for each cloth, as long as the number of foot-steps.

setup.art: A chair standing in an open doorway, with a dark room behind it and a black T-shirt hanging over its back.
setup.caption: 1. Hang a cloth on a chair in a doorway, with a dark room behind it.

setup.art: A phone torch with a folded white handkerchief held over it by a rubber band.
setup.caption: 2. Cover the torch with a folded hanky so it is dim, like a far-off headlight.

setup.art: A child in a dark room holding a dim torch beside her eye, stepping backwards heel to toe away from a chair with a cloth on it, a grown-up beside her.
setup.caption: 3. Hold the torch by your eye. Step back, heel to toe, until the cloth vanishes.

setup.art: A results table on paper with four rows for black, dark blue, yellow and white, and numbers of foot-steps.
setup.caption: 4. Count your foot-steps and write them down. Try each cloth twice.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Seen in the Dark test. Here you set up the chair and the dim torch.
flow.do: 1. Find the longest straight path in your home, ending at an open doorway. 2. Put the chair in the doorway, with the next room dark behind it. 3. Hang the black cloth over the chair back. 4. Fold the handkerchief into 4 layers and fix it over the torch with the rubber band.
flow.say: Tonight you are a driver, and this chair is a person walking on a dark road. The torch is your headlight. We make it dim, because a car's light is weak by the time it reaches someone far away.
flow.kid: Put the chair in a doorway. Keep the room behind it dark. Hang the black cloth on it. Cover the torch with the folded hanky.
flow.parent: The room behind the chair must be dark, with nothing pale behind the cloth, like a real road at night. If the wall behind is white, the black cloth shows up as a dark patch against it, and the test fails. If your home has no free doorway, hang a dark bedsheet behind the chair.

flow.do: 1. Show your child all the cloths in the light. 2. Ask for a guess and a reason. 3. Your child writes a guess in foot-steps for each cloth in the table.
flow.say: Which cloth do you think you will still see from furthest away? Which will vanish first? Why do you think so? Write a guess for each one.
flow.kid: Look at all the cloths. Which will you see from furthest away? Why? Write a guess for each one.

ask.q: Why do you think that cloth will be seen from furthest away?
good: It is bright.
White is easy to see.
Black looks like the dark.

flow.parent: Do not give the answer. Any guess with a reason is good. A foot-step is one shoe-length: put the heel of one foot against the toes of the other.

flow.do: 1. Switch off all the lights and close the curtains. 2. Wait 2 minutes so your eyes get used to the dark. 3. Your child stands 2 foot-steps from the chair, holding the dim torch against their cheek, pointing at the cloth.
flow.say: Let's wait two minutes in the dark. Your eyes need time to get used to it. Hold the torch right by your eye, like a headlight next to a driver.
flow.kid: Switch off the lights. Wait two minutes for your eyes. Hold the torch by your cheek. Point it at the cloth.
flow.parent: Phone screens and room lights must stay off, so every try has the same darkness.

flow.do: 1. Your child steps backwards, heel to toe, counting foot-steps, keeping the torch on the cloth. 2. They stop when they can no longer tell the cloth is there. 3. Write the number. 4. Switch on the light, change the cloth, switch off, and wait 1 minute. 5. Test every cloth this way.
flow.say: Step back slowly, heel to toe, and count. Keep the torch on the chair. Stop when you can't tell the cloth is there. How many foot-steps?
flow.kid: Step back, heel to toe. Count each step. Keep the torch on the cloth. Stop when it vanishes. Say the number.

ask.q: Which cloth vanished first? How far away were you?
good: The black one, after only a few steps.
The dark one went quickly.

flow.parent: Walk beside your child and keep one hand ready. If even the black cloth is still easy to see at the far end, add 2 more layers of hanky and start again. In many homes the black cloth vanishes within 2 to 5 foot-steps, and the white one may stay visible right to the far wall. If so, write 'still seen at' and the number.

flow.do: 1. Test each cloth a second time, in the same way. 2. Write the second numbers in the table.
flow.say: Scientists try each thing twice, because one try can be a fluke. Let's do every cloth again.
flow.kid: Test each cloth again. Write the new numbers. Are they close to the first ones?

flow.do: 1. If you have a reflective strip or a cycle reflector, put it on the chair. 2. Shine the dim torch from your eye. 3. Then hold the torch at arm's length to the side and look again. 4. Try a piece of kitchen foil the same way.
flow.say: Here is a reflective strip. Shine the torch from your eye. Now hold the torch far out to one side. Does the strip look the same?
flow.kid: Shine the torch at the strip from your eye. Now hold the torch far to the side. What changed?
flow.parent: The strip blazes when the torch is by the eye, and looks much duller when the torch is held to the side. It sends light back towards the lamp. Foil can glint brightly or look dark, depending on how it is tilted. Skip this step if you have no strip or reflector.

flow.do: 1. Switch the lights on. 2. Read the table together. 3. Ask your child for a claim, the evidence and a reason.
flow.say: What did you find? Which cloth could a driver see from furthest away? What is your evidence? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Which cloth did you see from furthest away? Which vanished first? Why do you think so?

ask.q: The same torch shone on every cloth. Why did some vanish sooner?
good: The black cloth sends back very little light.
The white cloth sends back more light to my eyes.

ask.q: What should you wear when you walk on a road at night?
good: White or pale clothes.
Something with a reflective strip.
Carry a torch.

check.q: Leela, a girl in Class 3, walks home at night in a black dress. Which change helps drivers see her from furthest away?
options: A white dupatta and a reflective strip on her bag
check.why: A driver sees Leela only by the headlight that bounces off her. A white dupatta reflects much more light than black, and a reflective strip sends the light straight back to the driver. Walking faster does not help the driver see her.

flow.think: You could see the torch's light the whole time. Why could you not see the black cloth?

experiments.title: Words Only: can you send a picture by talking?
experiments.context: In this experiment one person describes a simple picture and the other draws it without seeing it. You find out whether the drawing comes out better when the listener may ask questions.
experiments.question: Does a picture sent by words alone come out more correctly when the listener can ask questions, and does it take longer?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Will the drawing come out better when the listener stays silent, or when the listener can ask questions? Which way will be quicker? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use two pictures that are equally hard: each has the same 4 kinds of shapes in different places. The same person describes both times. Use a clock to time each round. Score each drawing in the same way, 2 points for each shape: 1 for the right shape and size, 1 for the right place. Then swap roles and do it again, using the pictures the other way round.

materials.item: 4 picture cards that you draw yourself (step 1 says how)
plain paper and a pencil for the listener
2 chairs placed back to back
a clock or a phone timer

schedule.what: Describe two pictures, one with a silent listener and one with questions allowed. Score and time both. Swap roles and repeat.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Put each drawing next to its picture card.

setup.art: A card with four simple shapes on it: a big circle top left, a small square inside it, a triangle bottom right and a straight line joining them.
setup.caption: 1. The describer holds a picture card the listener must not see.

setup.art: A girl and her father sitting on chairs back to back, the girl describing a card and the father drawing on paper.
setup.caption: 2. Sit back to back. One describes, the other draws.

setup.art: Two drawings side by side next to their picture cards, with ticks and crosses on the shapes.
setup.caption: 3. Compare each drawing with its card. Score 2 points for each shape.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Words Only test. Here you set up the chairs and the picture cards.
flow.do: 1. Put two chairs back to back. 2. The describer gets picture A and picture B, face down. 3. The listener gets paper and a pencil. 4. Ask for guesses and reasons.
flow.say: You will describe a picture using only words. I will draw it without seeing it. First, guess. Will my drawing be better if I stay silent, or if I can ask questions? Why?
flow.kid: Sit back to back. Hide your pictures. Guess: silent listener or questions allowed? Which will be better? Why?
flow.parent: If you cannot print, draw 4 cards. Each has 4 shapes: a circle, a square, a triangle and a straight line, in different sizes and places. Two cards are for the first go and two for the swap. Keep them simple.

flow.do: 1. Round 1: the describer describes picture A. 2. The listener draws and says nothing at all. 3. Time the round. 4. Stop when the describer says 'done'.
flow.say: Round 1. I must stay silent. I cannot ask anything. Describe picture A as clearly as you can. Tell me when you are done.
flow.kid: Describe picture A. Your listener must stay silent. Say 'done' at the end.
flow.parent: Do not nod, sigh or ask. This is one-way communication, like a radio programme.

flow.do: 1. Round 2: the describer describes picture B. 2. This time the listener may ask as many questions as they like. 3. Time the round.
flow.say: Round 2. Now I can ask questions. Describe picture B. I will ask whenever I am not sure.
flow.kid: Describe picture B. Now your listener can ask questions. Answer each one.
flow.parent: Ask real questions: 'How big is the circle?' 'Is the line touching the triangle?' This is two-way communication, like a phone call.

flow.do: 1. Turn the cards over. 2. Score each drawing: 2 points for each shape, 1 for the right shape and size, 1 for the right place. 3. Write the scores and times.
flow.say: Let's score them. For each shape, one point if it is the right shape and size, and one if it is in the right place.
flow.kid: Put each drawing next to its card. Give points for each shape. Write the scores and times.

ask.q: Which round had the higher score? Which was quicker?
good: The round with questions scored higher.
The silent round was quicker.

flow.do: 1. Swap roles: now the child draws. 2. Use the other two cards. Do one silent round and one round with questions. 3. Score and time both.
flow.say: Now I describe and you draw. We do it again, once silent and once with questions. Does the same thing happen?
flow.kid: Now you draw. Stay silent in the first round. Ask questions in the second. Score both.
flow.parent: Swapping checks that the result is not just because one of you is a better describer.

flow.do: Ask your child for a claim, the evidence and a reason.
flow.say: What did you find? What is your evidence? Why do you think questions made such a difference?
flow.kid: Which way gave better drawings? Which was quicker? Why do you think so?

ask.q: A road sign cannot answer questions. What does that mean for how it must be made?
good: It must be very simple.
Everyone must understand it at once.
It uses shapes and pictures, not long words.

check.q: Which of these is two-way communication?
check.why: On a phone call, both people can talk and ask questions. A road sign, a radio programme and a poster send a message only one way: you cannot answer them back.

activities.title: The Kitchen Journey: how far did our food travel?
activities.context: This is a quick start to the unit. You read where kitchen packets come from, and work out how they reached your home.

materials.item: 5 packets or things from the kitchen: rice, salt, tea, sugar, a soap, a fruit
a map of India, in a book or on a phone
paper and a pencil

schedule.what: Read 5 packets. Find each place on the map. Guess how each one travelled to your home.

activities.record: Make a list: the thing, where it came from, and how you think it travelled.

setup.art: Five kitchen packets on a table, a child's finger pointing at the small print on a tea packet.
setup.caption: 1. Read where each packet was made or packed.

setup.art: A map of India with dotted lines from Assam, Gujarat and Andhra Pradesh to a city in South India, with a truck, a train and a ship drawn on the lines.
setup.caption: 2. Find each place on the map. Draw how it travelled.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Kitchen Journey. You read where kitchen things come from.
flow.do: 1. Put 5 packets on the table. 2. Your child reads where each one was made or packed. 3. Find each place on the map.
flow.say: Almost nothing in our kitchen was made in our home. Let's read where these came from, and find each place on the map.
flow.kid: Read the small print on each packet. Where was it packed? Find the place on the map.

flow.do: 1. For each packet, ask how it reached your home. 2. Ask what the family would have if nothing could be carried from far away.
flow.say: How do you think this tea got from the hills to our shop? And from the shop to our home? What would we have if nothing could travel?
flow.kid: How did each thing get here? Truck, train, ship or scooter? What would we eat if nothing could travel?

ask.q: How did the tea get to our home?
good: By truck from the tea garden.
By train, then by the shop's van.
Someone carried it from the shop.

flow.parent: Good answers name more than one kind of transport, such as a train and then a truck. Tea often comes from the Nilgiris, Munnar or Assam. Salt often comes from Thoothukudi or Gujarat.

activities.title: The Time-line Rope: put transport and messages in order
activities.context: In this activity you put pictures of old and new transport and messages in order on a string, from oldest to newest.

materials.item: a long string or a dupatta, laid across the floor
12 small paper cards and a pencil
clothes pegs or tape

schedule.what: Draw 12 cards of transport and messages. Peg them on a string in order. Check the order together.

activities.record: Take a photo of your time-line, or copy it into your notebook.

setup.art: Twelve small hand-drawn cards: a footpath, a log boat, a bullock cart, a steam train, an aeroplane, a metro, a drum, a pigeon, a letter, a telephone, a radio and a mobile phone.
setup.caption: 1. Draw one thing on each card.

setup.art: A string stretched across a floor with the cards pegged on it in order from oldest to newest.
setup.caption: 2. Peg them on the string, oldest at one end.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Time-line Rope. You make 12 picture cards.
flow.do: 1. Draw one thing on each of 12 cards. 2. Draw a footpath, a log boat, a bullock cart, a steam train, a bus and an aeroplane. 3. Draw a drum, a messenger pigeon, a letter, a telephone, a radio and a mobile phone.
flow.say: Let's draw twelve ways people have travelled and sent messages. Keep each drawing quick and simple.
flow.kid: Draw one thing on each card. Keep each drawing small and quick.

flow.do: 1. Your child pegs the cards on the string in the order they think they were invented. 2. Then read the 'How transport grew' and 'How communication grew' cards together and fix the order.
flow.say: Put them in order, oldest at this end and newest at that end. Which do you think came first, the boat or the wheel?
flow.kid: Peg the cards in order. Oldest at one end. Newest at the other. Which came first, the boat or the wheel?
flow.parent: Boats came long before wheels. A log canoe found in the Netherlands is about 10,000 years old. The oldest wheels are about 5,500 years old. Messengers and drums came long before letters and the post.

flow.do: Ask what each new invention made possible.
flow.say: Pick one card. What could people do after this was invented that they could not do before?
flow.kid: Pick one card. What could people do after it was invented?

check.q: Which of these is the oldest?
check.why: Boats are much older than wheels. Log canoes about 10,000 years old have been found. Wheels came about 5,500 years ago, trains about 200 years ago and aeroplanes about 120 years ago.

activities.title: Sign Spotting: read the road signs near home
activities.context: In this activity you walk with a grown-up along a road near home and spot road signs and signals. You sort them by shape.

materials.item: a notebook and pencil
a phone camera, if you have one

activities.safety: A grown-up holds the child's hand on the road. Stay on the footpath. Stop to look and draw only in a safe place, never at the road's edge.

schedule.what: Walk along a nearby road with a grown-up. Draw every road sign you see. Sort them into circles, triangles and rectangles at home.

activities.record: Draw each sign you saw. Write what it means. Sort them into three groups: circles (orders), triangles (warnings) and rectangles (information).

setup.art: A grown-up and a child on a footpath, the child pointing at a round 'No horn' sign near a hospital gate.
setup.caption: 1. Walk on the footpath with a grown-up. Look for signs.

setup.art: A notebook page with three columns, headed circle, triangle and rectangle, with small drawings of road signs in each.
setup.caption: 2. At home, sort your signs by shape.

flow.context: This is the first step of Sign Spotting. You walk with a grown-up and look for road signs.
flow.do: 1. Walk on the footpath along a busy road near home. 2. Stop in a safe place each time your child spots a sign or signal. 3. They draw it, or you photograph it.
flow.say: Let's be sign spotters. Every time you see a road sign or a signal, tell me. We will stop somewhere safe to draw it.
flow.kid: Hold the grown-up's hand. Look for road signs. Say 'sign!' when you see one.
flow.parent: Look near schools, hospitals, junctions, bus stops and speed breakers. Zebra crossings and the pedestrian lights at a signal count too.

flow.do: 1. At home, sort the signs into circles, triangles and rectangles. 2. Read the 'Road signs and traffic lights' card to check the meanings.
flow.say: Let's sort your signs by shape. What do all the circles have in common? What about the triangles?
flow.kid: Sort your signs into circles, triangles and rectangles. What does each shape mean?

ask.q: What does a red-bordered triangle tell a driver?
good: Be careful, something is ahead.
It is a warning.

activities.title: Torch Code: send a word across the room without a sound
activities.context: In this activity you invent a code of short and long torch flashes, like the old telegraph, and send a word across the room.

materials.item: a torch, or a phone torch
paper and a pencil

activities.safety: Never shine the torch into anyone's eyes. Point it at the wall or the ceiling.

schedule.what: Make a code for 6 letters. Send a short word by torch flashes. Swap and try again.

activities.record: Write your code on a card. Write which words got through correctly and which did not.

setup.art: A card with six letters, each with a pattern of dots and dashes beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Make a code: a pattern of short and long flashes for each letter.

setup.art: A child in a dim room flashing a torch at the ceiling, and her mother across the room writing letters on paper.
setup.caption: 2. Flash a word at the ceiling. Your partner writes it down.

flow.context: This is the first step of Torch Code. You make a code of short and long flashes.
flow.do: 1. Together, choose 6 letters, such as A, E, I, P, T and N. 2. Give each one a different pattern of short and long flashes. 3. Both of you copy the code.
flow.say: Long ago, the telegraph sent messages as short and long pulses. We will make our own code with a torch. Give each letter its own pattern.
flow.kid: Pick six letters. Give each one a pattern. Short flash is a dot. Long flash is a dash.

flow.do: 1. Dim the lights. 2. Your child flashes a 3-letter word at the ceiling, such as PAN or TEN. 3. You write down the letters. 4. Swap.
flow.say: Flash your word at the ceiling. Wait a little between letters, so I know where one ends.
flow.kid: Flash your word at the ceiling. Pause between letters. Did your partner get it?

ask.q: What went wrong when a word did not get through?
good: The pause between letters was too short.
Two letters had codes that looked alike.

flow.do: Talk about how the real telegraph and today's phones send messages as patterns.
flow.say: The telegraph used a code like ours, called Morse code, sent along wires. Your phone still sends messages as patterns, much faster. What is good about a code? What is hard?
flow.kid: Your phone sends messages as fast patterns too. What was hard about your code?
flow.parent: In Morse code, the letter S is three short signals. It was the first letter Marconi reported hearing across the Atlantic in 1901.

activities.title: Window Traffic Count: how many people does each vehicle carry?
activities.context: In this activity you watch the road from a window or balcony, and count vehicles and the people inside them.

materials.item: a window or balcony that looks onto a road
a tally sheet and a pencil

activities.safety: Stay well back from the balcony rail. A grown-up stays with you.

schedule.what: For 10 minutes, tally cars, two-wheelers, autos and buses, and count the people in each. Work out people per vehicle.

activities.record: Make a tally table: vehicle, how many passed, and how many people you counted in them.

setup.art: A child at a balcony with a grown-up, looking at a road with a bus, cars, two-wheelers and an auto.
setup.caption: 1. Watch the road for 10 minutes.

setup.art: A tally sheet with rows for car, two-wheeler, auto and bus, and tally marks for vehicles and for people.
setup.caption: 2. Tally each vehicle, and the people you can see inside.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Window Traffic Count. You tally vehicles and people for 10 minutes.
flow.do: 1. Set a timer for 10 minutes. 2. For each car, two-wheeler and auto, make a tally mark and count the people you can see. 3. For a bus, guess roughly how full it is.
flow.say: For ten minutes, let's count vehicles. For each one, also count the people in it. For a bus, guess if it is empty, half full or full.
flow.kid: Make a tally mark for each vehicle. Count the people in it. Is the bus full?
flow.parent: A full city bus can carry about 50 or more people. Your child cannot count them, so a rough guess is fine.

flow.do: Compare how many people each kind of vehicle carried, and how much road it took up.
flow.say: How many cars passed? How many people were in them? One bus took about as much road as how many cars?
flow.kid: Which vehicle carried most people? Which made the most smoke for each person?

ask.q: Why might a city want more buses and fewer cars?
good: A bus carries many people in one vehicle.
Less smoke and less traffic for each person.

activities.title: Ask a Grandparent: how did you travel and send messages at my age?
activities.context: In this activity you phone or visit a grandparent or an older neighbour and ask how they travelled and sent messages when they were young.

materials.item: a phone, or a visit
a notebook and pencil

schedule.what: Interview a grandparent with 5 questions. Write down their answers. Compare their childhood with yours.

activities.record: Write a short 'then and now' table with their answers and yours.

setup.art: A girl on a video call with her grandmother, a notebook open on her lap.
setup.caption: 1. Call a grandparent and ask your questions.

setup.art: A notebook page with two columns, 'Paati, then' and 'Me, now', and short answers about school, trains and letters.
setup.caption: 2. Write a 'then and now' table.

flow.context: This is the first step of Ask a Grandparent. You interview an older person about travel and messages long ago.
flow.do: 1. Help your child write 5 questions. 2. Your child asks them on the phone or in person. 3. They write short answers.
flow.say: Ask: How did you get to school? What was your first train journey? How did you send news to relatives? When did you first use a phone? When did you first watch TV?
flow.kid: Ask your five questions. Listen well. Write a few words for each answer.
flow.parent: Many grandparents in India remember telegrams for urgent news, postcards, long-distance trunk calls booked through the telephone exchange, and the first TV in the street.

flow.do: Fill in the 'then and now' table together.
flow.say: Let's compare. What is faster now? Is anything better about how it was then?
flow.kid: Fill in your table. What is faster now? Was anything better then?

projects.title: Our Safe Walk Map: the route to the nearest shop
projects.context: In this 2-day project you walk the route to a nearby shop with a grown-up, then draw a map that shows the safe crossings, the signs and the dark places.

materials.item: a notebook and pencil
a large sheet of paper and coloured pencils
a torch, for the evening walk

projects.safety: A grown-up walks with the child both times and holds their hand at crossings. Do the evening walk before it is fully dark.

schedule.what: Walk to the shop in daylight. Note the crossings, signs and signals. Note where the footpath is broken or missing.
Walk the same route at dusk with a torch. Note the dark places. Draw the map with symbols and a key.

projects.record: Draw the map. Use a symbol for each crossing, sign, signal and dark spot, and explain them in a key.

setup.art: A child and a grown-up on a footpath, the child writing in a notebook next to a zebra crossing.
setup.caption: 1. Walk the route in daylight. Note every crossing and sign.

setup.art: The same street at dusk, the child shining a torch at the ground and pointing at a dark corner without a street light.
setup.caption: 2. Walk it again at dusk. Find the dark places.

setup.art: A hand-drawn map with a home, a shop, zebra stripes, small sign symbols, black dots for dark spots, and a key in the corner.
setup.caption: 3. Draw the map with a key.

flow.context: This is day 1 of the Safe Walk Map. You walk to the shop in daylight and note what keeps walkers safe.
flow.do: 1. Walk to the nearest shop with your child. 2. At each crossing, signal or sign, stop and let your child note it. 3. Note where walkers must step onto the road.
flow.say: Today we are road checkers. Where are the safe places to cross? Where must we walk on the road? Let's note them all.
flow.kid: Hold hands. Note every crossing, signal and sign. Where is there no footpath?

flow.context: This is day 2 of the Safe Walk Map. You walk the same route at dusk.
flow.do: 1. Walk the same route at dusk, with a torch. 2. Note dark spots with no street light. 3. Notice which walkers you see easily.
flow.say: Now it is getting dark. Where can drivers not see us well? Which people on the road can you see easily, and why?
flow.kid: Shine the torch at the ground. Where is it darkest? Who is easy to see?
flow.wait: Do this on day 2, at dusk.

flow.do: Draw the map with a key, at home.
flow.say: Let's draw the map. Make a symbol for crossings, signals, signs and dark spots, and put them in a key.
flow.kid: Draw your home and the shop. Add the crossings, signs and dark spots. Make a key.

ask.q: If a friend walked this way at night, what would you tell them?
good: Cross at the zebra crossing.
Wear something white and carry a torch.
Be careful at the dark corner.

challenges.title: A Sign Without Words
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. You design a sign that everyone understands at once, even someone who cannot read.
challenges.problem: Your building needs a sign at the gate that says: 'Children play here. Drive slowly.' Many visitors and drivers do not read English, Tamil or Hindi. Design a sign that anyone understands in two seconds.
constraints: It must be understood in 2 seconds, from 5 steps away.
Use the shape and colour rules that road signs use.
general: Use a triangle with a red border, because a triangle means a warning.
Draw two running children in black, like the real 'School ahead' sign.
Add a red circle with '10' to give a speed limit.
creative: Test the sign on three people: show it for two seconds, then ask what it means.
Make it bigger and simpler after each test.
Stick a strip of foil or reflective tape on the border so it shines in headlights.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own sign for something in your building or street. Show it for 2 seconds to three people. Did they all understand it?

setup.art: A child drawing a red-bordered triangle with two running children on a sheet of card.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a sign with no words.

setup.art: The child holding the sign up for two seconds while her grandmother, five steps away, guesses its meaning.
setup.caption: 2. Show it for 2 seconds from 5 steps away. Do people understand?

flow.do: Your child sketches three ideas, using shapes and colours from real road signs.
flow.say: A driver has two seconds to read your sign. What shape should it be? What picture? Draw three ideas.
flow.kid: Draw three ideas. What shape? What colour? What picture?

flow.do: Show the best sign to three people for 2 seconds each, from 5 steps away. Write what they say.
flow.say: Hold it up for just two seconds. Then ask, 'What does it mean?'
flow.kid: Show your sign for two seconds. Ask what it means. Write their answers.

flow.do: Improve the sign and test again.
flow.say: What confused people? How can you make it simpler?
flow.kid: Fix what confused people. Test it again.

check.q: Which shape should a warning sign be, in India?
check.why: In India, a triangle with a red border warns drivers of something ahead. Circles give orders and rectangles give information.

challenges.title: Be Seen: a night band for a school bag
challenges.context: This is an engineering challenge. You make a band for a school bag that drivers can see from far away at night, using things from home.
challenges.problem: A child walks home from tuition after dark. Make a band for their school bag that a driver can see from as far away as possible, using only things from home. Test it with the dim torch from the Seen in the Dark test.
constraints: It must not fall off when the bag is shaken.
Test it in the dark with the dim torch, from your eye, and count foot-steps.
materials: a steel lid or an old CD
the dim torch from the Seen in the Dark test
general: Use a strip of white cloth: white reflects much more light than dark colours.
Use a reflective strip or tape, which sends light back towards the driver.
Make the band wide: a bigger white area is seen from further away.
creative: Crumple kitchen foil, then smooth it flat, so it glints from many angles.
Cut an old CD into strips with a grown-up's help: it shines in many directions.
Put bands on both the front and the back, so drivers coming either way can see them.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own night band. Test it in the dark. How many foot-steps away can you still see it? Can you beat the white cloth?

setup.art: A school bag with a band of white cloth and crumpled foil taped across it.
setup.caption: 1. Make a band from white cloth, foil or other shiny things.

setup.art: A child in a dark room holding a dim torch by her eye, stepping back from a chair with the school bag on it.
setup.caption: 2. Test it with the dim torch. Count foot-steps.

flow.do: Your child chooses materials and makes a band for the bag.
flow.say: Think back to the dark-room test. What did a driver see from furthest away? Use that to design your band.
flow.kid: Remember the dark test. What did you see from furthest away? Make your band.
flow.parent: Help with scissors. If you cut a CD, a grown-up does the cutting, because the edges can be sharp.

flow.do: Test the band in the dark with the dim torch, from your eye, as in the Seen in the Dark test. Count foot-steps.
flow.say: Let's test it in the dark. Step back until you can't see the band. How far?
flow.kid: Test your band in the dark. Count your foot-steps. Beat the white cloth?

flow.do: Talk about what worked best and why.
flow.say: Which part of your band shone furthest? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Which part shone furthest? Why?
