quiz.p: Which kind of transport is a goods train?
quiz.why: A train runs on rails, so it is rail transport.
Boats are about 10,000 years old or more. Trains, cars and aeroplanes are all less than 250 years old.

quiz.p: Indu, a girl in Class 3 in Hyderabad, will walk home after dark. Which clothes help drivers see her from furthest away?
opts: A white frock with a reflective strip on her bag
quiz.why: White reflects much more of a car's headlight than dark colours, and a reflective strip sends the light straight back to the driver. Picking a dark colour means thinking the driver sees the person, not the light coming back from her.

quiz.p: What does a red-bordered triangle on a road sign tell a driver?
quiz.why: In India, a triangle with a red border is a warning sign, such as 'School ahead' or 'Speed breaker'.

quiz.p: The traffic light shows amber. What should a driver do?
quiz.why: Amber means the light is about to turn red, so get ready to stop.

quiz.p: Which of these is one-way communication?
quiz.why: You can listen to a radio programme, but you cannot ask it questions. The other three are two-way.

quiz.p: Why must a road sign be very simple?
opts: A driver sees it for only a moment and cannot ask what it means
quiz.why: A road sign is one-way communication, read in a moment. In the Words Only test, the silent listener made more mistakes, so one-way messages must be very clear.

quiz.p: Which of these makes no exhaust at all?
quiz.why: A cycle burns no fuel, so it makes no exhaust. Petrol and diesel engines give out smoke and gases.

quiz.p: What is the cheapest way to carry very heavy goods across the sea?
quiz.why: Ships carry huge loads cheaply, though slowly. Aeroplanes are fast but cost far more.

quiz.p: Which invention first sent messages as electric pulses along wires?
quiz.why: The telegraph sent short and long pulses of electricity along wires, in a code such as Morse code.

quiz.p: A sign is a red circle with '30' inside. What does it mean?
opts: Do not go faster than 30 kilometres an hour
quiz.why: A red circle gives an order. A number inside it is a speed limit in kilometres an hour.

quiz.p: One full bus carries about as many people as 25 cars. Why is that good for the city's air?
opts: One engine burns far less fuel than 25 engines
quiz.why: One bus engine burns much less fuel than 25 car engines. So sharing a bus makes much less smoke for each person.

worksheets.title: Transport, messages and road safety (core)
worksheets.context: This worksheet checks the main ideas: kinds of transport, road signs, one-way and two-way messages, and being seen at night.

items.p: Meenakshi, a girl in Class 3 in Madurai, makes a list of ways to travel. Sort each one into its kind of transport.
items.a: see items
items.why: Road transport runs on roads, rail on tracks, water transport floats, and air transport flies. A kattumaram is a raft of logs tied together. A strong answer knows that a metro is rail transport, even when it runs on a bridge above the road.

items.p: In the Seen in the Dark test, Divya shone the same dim torch on a black cloth and a white cloth. Which one could she still see from further away?
items.why: The white cloth reflects much more of the torch light back to Divya's eyes, so she can still see it from further away. The black cloth reflects very little, so it vanishes sooner.

items.p: Arjun says, 'I can see the car's headlights, so the driver can see me.' Explain why he may be wrong.
items.a: Arjun sees the bright lamp itself. The driver sees Arjun only by the little light that bounces off him and comes back. If Arjun wears dark clothes, very little light comes back, so the driver may not see him.
items.why: A strong answer says that seeing a lamp and being seen by its light are different. It uses the idea of light bouncing off and coming back.

items.p: A traffic light that is ____ means stop.
items.why: Red means stop, amber means get ready to stop, and green means go.

items.p: Match each road sign shape to what it tells you.
pairs: useful information, such as the way to a petrol pump
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: In India, circles give orders, triangles warn, and rectangles give information. A strong answer could draw one example of each.

items.p: Boats were invented long before wheels.
items.why: True. Log canoes about 10,000 years old have been found. The oldest wheels are about 5,500 years old. Many people guess the wheel came first.

items.p: Draw a road sign that warns drivers that a school is ahead. Colour its border.
items.a: A triangle with a red border, a white middle, and two children drawn in black.
items.why: A warning sign is a red-bordered triangle. The picture of children tells drivers to slow down and watch out.

items.p: Which of these is two-way communication?
items.why: In a talk, both of you can speak and ask questions. A newspaper, a billboard and TV news send a message one way only.

items.p: Put these ways of sending messages in order, from oldest to newest.
items.why: Messengers on foot are thousands of years old. The telegraph came in the 1800s, radio in the early 1900s, and mobile phones in India in 1995.

items.p: Name two ways that cars and buses harm the air or our health.
items.a: Their exhaust has tiny specks of soot and harmful gases that hurt our lungs. It also has carbon dioxide, which warms the Earth. Horns and engines make noise pollution too.
items.why: A strong answer names two different harms, such as dirty air and noise, or harm to lungs and warming of the Earth.

items.p: Selvi, a girl in Class 3, wants to send a photo to her cousin in Kolkata right now. Which is the quickest way?
opts: Send it by phone over the internet
Give it to a train passenger
items.why: The internet carries a photo in seconds. A letter or courier takes days.

items.p: Two friends in Chennai are going to a shop 1 kilometre away, on a hot afternoon.

views.says: We should walk. It makes no smoke and no noise, and it is good exercise.
We should take an auto. It is hot, and it is faster.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Give a reason. Then say one thing the other friend has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side and gives a reason, such as no pollution, or saving time in the heat. It also gives the other friend their due: walking is clean and healthy, and an auto is quicker and easier in great heat or with heavy bags.
items.why: There is a real trade-off between clean travel and quick, comfortable travel. A good answer weighs both.

items.p: Which of these is NOT a means of communication?
items.why: A bullock cart carries people and goods. It is transport. Letters, phone calls and radio carry messages.

items.p: Label the three lights of a traffic signal with what each one means.
items.why: The red light is at the top, amber in the middle and green at the bottom. A strong answer writes what each colour tells the driver to do.
items.art: A traffic signal with three empty circles.

items.p: Your family walks home after dinner at night. Write two things each person can do so that drivers see them.
items.a: Wear white or pale clothes. Wear or carry something with a reflective strip. Carry a torch and shine it on the ground ahead.
items.why: A strong answer uses the Seen in the Dark test: pale clothes and reflective strips send much more light back to a driver.

worksheets.title: Signs, signals and choices (stretch)
worksheets.context: This worksheet goes further: reflective signs, one-way messages, choosing transport, and how radio crosses the Earth.

items.p: In the Seen in the Dark test, Nandini held a reflective strip on the chair. It shone brightly when the torch was beside her eye. What happened when she held the torch far out to the side?
items.why: A reflective strip sends light straight back towards the lamp. With the torch by her eye, the light came straight back to her. With the torch to the side, the light went back to the torch, not to her eyes.

items.p: Many road signs are covered with reflective sheeting. Why does this help a driver at night?
items.a: The sheeting sends the car's headlight straight back towards the driver. So the sign shines brightly to the driver, even though no lamp is switched on inside it.
items.why: A strong answer says where the light comes from (the car's own headlights) and where it goes (back to the driver).

items.p: In the Words Only test, Revathi described a picture to her mother. In which round did her mother's drawing probably score higher?
opts: When her mother had to stay silent
When her mother could ask questions
Scores have nothing to do with questions
items.why: When the listener can ask, she can clear up mistakes, such as which shape is bigger. Two-way communication usually gets more right, but it takes longer.

items.p: A driver passes a road sign in two seconds. Use what you found in the Words Only test to explain why a road sign must be very simple.
items.a: A road sign is one-way communication. The driver cannot ask it what it means. In the test, the silent listener made more mistakes. So a sign must be simple enough to understand at once, with no questions.
items.why: A strong answer links the sign to one-way communication and uses evidence from the test.

items.p: Sort these into one-way and two-way communication.
items.a: see items
items.why: In two-way communication, both sides can send and receive. Letters sent back and forth are two-way, but slow.

items.p: Which is the best way to carry petrol from a refinery to a city 300 kilometres away, every day, for years?
items.why: A pipeline carries liquid all day and night, without any vehicle. Once it is built, it is cheap and safe for this job.

items.p: Electric scooters give out no exhaust on the road, but their electricity may still cause pollution somewhere else.
items.why: True. In India, much electricity is made by burning coal in power stations. So the pollution moves from the road to the power station.

items.p: A town council in Kerala is deciding how to spend money on transport.

views.says: Build a wider road, so more cars can come to the market.
Build footpaths and cycle lanes, so people walk and cycle, and the air is cleaner.
Run more buses, so people without cars can travel too.

items.ask: Which plan would you choose? Give two reasons. Then say what is good about one of the other plans.
items.a: A strong answer chooses a plan and gives two reasons, such as clean air, cost, or who can use it. It then fairly names a strength of another plan, for example that a wider road helps trucks bring goods to shops.
items.why: Real towns weigh these trade-offs. More road space often fills with more cars. Footpaths and buses help people without cars. There is no single right answer.

items.p: The 6-digit number in an Indian address that helps the post office sort letters is called the ____.
items.why: PIN stands for Postal Index Number. PIN codes began in India in 1972.

items.p: Draw a map of a road crossing near a school. Put a zebra crossing, a 'School ahead' sign and a traffic light where they should go.
items.a: A crossroads with zebra stripes at the crossing near the school gate, a red-bordered triangle with children placed before the school on each side, and a traffic light at the junction.
items.why: Warning signs must come before the danger, so drivers have time to slow down. A strong drawing puts the sign some way before the school, not at its gate.
items.art: A blank outline of two crossing roads and a school building.

items.p: Radio waves travel in straight lines. Yet a radio station far beyond the curve of the Earth can sometimes be heard. Why?
opts: Radio waves curl around the Earth by themselves
A charged layer high in the air sends some radio waves back down
Radio waves travel through the ground
items.why: The ionosphere, a layer of charged air high above us, sends some radio waves back down to the ground. Edward Appleton showed this in 1924.

items.p: Choose one invention from this unit: the wheel, the train, the telegraph or the mobile phone. What could people do after it that they could not do before?
items.a: For example: after the train, people could travel across India in days instead of weeks, and carry heavy goods like coal and rice cheaply to faraway cities.
items.why: A strong answer names a real change and says why the invention made it possible.

items.p: Put these in order, from oldest to newest.
items: The first passenger train in India
a: The first passenger train in India
items.why: Log boats are about 10,000 years old. Wheels are about 5,500 years old. India's first passenger train ran in 1853. Kochi's water metro began in 2023.

items.p: Three of these are warning signs. Which is the odd one out?
opts: A triangle with a speed breaker
A triangle with a sharp bend
A red circle with a crossed-out horn
items.why: The red circle is an order: do not sound your horn. The triangles all warn of something ahead.

items.p: A honeybee finds flowers and comes back to the hive. How does she tell other bees where the flowers are?
opts: She dances, and the direction and length of her dance show the way
She buzzes the name of the flower
items.why: Honeybees dance on the comb. The direction of the dance shows which way to fly, and its length shows how far. Karl von Frisch worked this out.

worksheets.title: Thinking like a road engineer (challenge)
worksheets.context: This worksheet asks you to plan tests, weigh trade-offs and argue from evidence.

items.p: In the Seen in the Dark test, the white cloth was seen from much further away than the black cloth. On a real road, why does this distance matter so much to a driver going fast?
items.a: A fast vehicle needs a long distance to slow down and stop. If the driver sees a walker only when very close, there is no time to stop. Seeing someone from further away gives the driver time.
items.why: A strong answer links seeing distance to stopping distance, and so to safety.

items.p: In the Seen in the Dark test, Kavya's white cloth was still visible at the far wall, 15 foot-steps away. What should she do to find how far it can really be seen?
opts: Make the torch dimmer, or use a longer room, and test all the cloths again
Test only the white cloth again
items.why: If the white cloth is still seen at the wall, she has not found its limit. A dimmer torch or a longer room lets her find it. She must test every cloth again in the same way, so the test stays fair.

items.p: After the Seen in the Dark test, three people talk about road safety at night.

views.says: Walkers must wear pale clothes and reflective strips. Then drivers will see them.
Drivers must slow down at night, because they cannot see everyone, whatever they wear.
The town must put up street lights and footpaths, so people do not walk on dark roads at all.

items.ask: Who do you think has the most important point? Use evidence from your test. Then explain why the other two still matter.
items.a: A strong answer uses the test, for example that the black cloth vanished at a few steps. It may choose any person, but it sees that all three help: being seen, driving slowly, and safer roads work together.
items.why: Road safety depends on walkers, drivers and the town together. A good answer weighs each.

items.p: Many people think bright neon colours are best at night. Plan a test in a dark room to check this. Say what you would compare, and what would make it fair.
items.a: I would compare a neon green or orange cloth with a white cloth and a reflective strip, using the dim torch by my eye. Same chair, same darkness, same torch, two tries each. I would count foot-steps until each vanished.
items.why: A strong plan keeps everything the same except the cloth, and tries each one more than once.

items.p: In the Words Only test, Pooja's silent round took 2 minutes and scored 3 out of 8. Her question round took 5 minutes and scored 7 out of 8. What does this show?
opts: Two-way communication got more right but took longer
items.why: The question round scored 4 more points but took 3 more minutes. Two-way communication is usually more correct and slower. That is a real trade-off.

items.p: A cyclone warning goes out by radio and TV. Is that one-way or two-way communication? What problem could that cause, and how could it be fixed?
items.a: It is one-way. People cannot ask questions, such as 'Where is the nearest shelter?' It could be fixed by giving a phone helpline, or by local volunteers who go to each street and answer questions.
items.why: A strong answer names it as one-way and suggests adding a two-way channel.

items.p: Marconi was the only person who worked on early radio.
items.why: False. Many people worked on radio. In Kolkata in the 1890s, J.C. Bose made and detected very short radio waves. Tesla, Popov and others also built radio devices.

items.p: Draw the curved Earth with two radio towers far apart. Show how a radio wave can travel from one to the other by bouncing off the ionosphere.
items.a: A curved Earth, a layer above it marked ionosphere, and a zigzag line from one tower up to the layer, down to the ground, and up and down again to the far tower.
items.why: A strong drawing shows straight lines that change direction at the ionosphere, not a wave that curves by itself.
items.art: A curved line for the Earth's surface with two small towers far apart.

items.p: One full bus carries 50 people. Each car carries 2 people. How many cars would carry the same people as one full bus?
items.why: 50 people divided by 2 people in each car is 25 cars. That is why one full bus takes far less road space and fuel for each person than cars.

items.p: The wheel was invented about 5,500 years ago, but in some hilly places people kept carrying loads on their backs or on animals for thousands of years more. Why might wheels not help much there?
items.a: Wheels need smooth, fairly flat ground or roads. On steep, rocky paths a cart cannot go, but a person or a donkey can.
items.why: A strong answer sees that an invention helps only where its conditions are right.

items.p: Sort each change by whether it would make city air cleaner or dirtier.
items.a: see items
items.why: Fewer engines burning fuel for each person means cleaner air. Jams and idling engines burn fuel without going anywhere.

items.p: A message travelling from Earth to a faraway spacecraft takes about a day to arrive. What does this mean for talking to it?
opts: You can chat with it like a phone call
Every question takes about two days to get an answer
items.why: The question takes about a day to get there and the answer about a day to come back. So conversation is very slow, more like letters than a phone call.

items.p: Some biologists say plants communicate when they release smells that warn their neighbours. Others prefer the word 'signalling'. What do you think counts as communication? Give a reason.
items.a: A strong answer gives a clear view and a reason, for example: 'It is communication, because one plant sends a message and another plant acts on the message, just like a crow's warning call.'
items.why: There is a real debate about the words. A good answer says what it thinks communication needs: a sender, a message and a receiver who acts.

items.p: Label the parts of a message's journey on a phone call.
a: radio waves reach a phone tower
the tower sends it on through cables or a satellite
it reaches another tower and then your friend's phone
items.why: A phone call is carried as radio waves to the nearest tower, then on through cables or satellites, then out again by radio to the other phone. A strong answer puts the parts in the right order.
items.art: Two phones far apart with a tower near each, and a cable and a satellite between the towers.

items: A postwoman brings it to the door

open_questions.q: Who really sent the first radio signals, and who deserves the most credit?
open_questions.why_open: Bose, Marconi, Tesla, Popov and others all did important early work at about the same time. Historians still argue about how to share the credit.

open_questions.q: Did Marconi really hear the signal across the Atlantic in 1901?
open_questions.why_open: Only Marconi and his assistant heard the faint clicks, and nothing was recorded. Some engineers have argued that he may have heard noise. Later tests by his company did work across the ocean.

open_questions.q: How can our cities move everyone quickly without dirtying the air?
open_questions.why_open: Metros, buses, electric vehicles, cycle lanes and working from home all help, but every city is different and nobody has found one answer that works everywhere.

open_questions.q: Exactly how do nearby plants respond to the warning smells of a plant being eaten?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have found that neighbours get their defences ready, but they are still working out which smells matter and how plants sense them.

open_questions.q: Where did the wheel first come from?
open_questions.why_open: Very old wheels have been found in Mesopotamia, near the Black Sea and in Europe, all about 5,000 to 5,500 years old. Nobody knows for sure where the first one was made.

maths.problem: In the Seen in the Dark test, Kavya still saw the white shirt from 15 foot-steps away. The black T-shirt vanished at 3 foot-steps. How many times further away was the white shirt seen?
maths.explain: The white shirt was seen at 15 foot-steps and the black T-shirt at 3. 15 divided by 3 is 5. So the white shirt was seen 5 times further away. Check: 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 15.
maths.context: This is about the Seen in the Dark test. In a dark room, you step back from a cloth with a dim torch until the cloth vanishes.

chart.title: How far away each cloth could be seen

maths.why_maths: Saying 'five times further' tells a driver much more than saying 'white is better'.

maths.problem: Kavya's yellow dupatta was seen at 12 foot-steps on try 1 and 14 foot-steps on try 2. What is the middle value of her two tries?
maths.explain: 12 + 14 = 26. Half of 26 is 13. So the middle value is 13 foot-steps. This is called the average of the two tries.
maths.context: This is about the Seen in the Dark test, where each cloth is tested twice.
maths.why_maths: Two tries rarely give the same number. Taking the middle value gives one fair number for each cloth.

maths.problem: Farhan watched the road for 10 minutes. He counted 20 cars with 2 people in each, and 1 bus with about 40 people. Which carried more people: all the cars together, or the one bus?
maths.answer: They carried the same number: 40 people each.
maths.explain: 20 cars with 2 people each is 20 × 2 = 40 people. The bus carried about 40 people too. So one bus carried as many people as 20 cars, using one engine instead of 20.
maths.context: This is about the Window Traffic Count, where you count vehicles and the people in them.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying shows how many people each kind of vehicle really carries, so you can compare them fairly.

maths.problem: India's first passenger train ran in 1853. Kochi's water metro began in 2023. How many years apart are they?
maths.explain: 2023 − 1853 = 170. Count up: from 1853 to 1953 is 100 years, and from 1953 to 2023 is 70 more. 100 + 70 = 170.
maths.context: This is about the Time-line Rope, where you put transport inventions in order.
maths.why_maths: Working out the gap between dates shows how fast transport has changed.

maths.problem: In the Words Only test, Revathi's silent round took 2 minutes and scored 3 out of 8. Her question round took 5 minutes and scored 7 out of 8. How many more points did questions give? How many more minutes did they take?
maths.explain: 7 − 3 = 4 more points. 5 − 2 = 3 more minutes. So questions gave a much better drawing, but took longer. Whether it is worth it depends on the job.
maths.context: This is about the Words Only test, where one person describes a picture and the other draws it without seeing it.
maths.why_maths: Comparing both the gain and the cost helps us choose: a quick message or a correct one.

roots.context: We have learned how people, goods and messages travel, and found in the dark that a driver sees us only by the light we send back. Now we ask what this tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: With the same dim torch, the black cloth vanished a few steps away. The white cloth was still clear across the room. Both were there the whole time. A driver knows you are on the road only when light from you reaches their eyes.
deep_truth.habit: We think that being somewhere is the same as being seen there, and that if we can see a car, its driver can see us. The test showed that being seen depends on how much light comes back from us. Road safety needs both: we must see, and we must be seen.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Seen in the Dark test, every cloth stayed on the chair and got the same torch light. Only the light reflected back to the eye changed, and the black cloth vanished first. A reflective strip, which sends light straight back to the lamp, shone brightest of all.

three.who_am_i: Others see you only by the light that bounces off you into their eyes. Your face reaches your friend as light.
three.what_is_life: Bees dance, ants leave smell trails, crows call and plants release smells that warn their neighbours. Living beings are always sending messages.
three.what_is_this_world: Roads, rails, wires and radio waves join far places, so rice from Andhra Pradesh reaches a kitchen in Kochi.

roots.thread: Every message needs a sender, something that carries it, and a receiver. In the dark test, the torch, the cloth and your eye made one chain, and if any part was missing, nothing was seen. Roads, rails, wires and radio waves are longer chains of the same kind. Light, sound and signals pass between things all the time, so no part of the world is ever fully cut off from the rest. One world shows up as many separate things, and they stay in touch through what passes between them.

other_view.view: The Charvakas taught that perception, what our senses show us, is the only sure way to know anything. In the dark, you could not see the black cloth. playtest: Every experiment, activity, game, challenge and project was walked through as if at home, with the listed materials. The Seen in the Dark test depends on two things: a dark background behind the cloth, and a dim enough torch. With a bare phone torch, even a black cloth may stay visible across a small room, so the torch is covered with a hanky folded into 4 layers, and the step says to add layers if needed. If a white wall is behind the chair, the black cloth shows up as a dark shape, so the chair stands in a doorway with a dark room behind it, or in front of a dark bedsheet. The child steps back heel to toe, which gives about 15 to 25 foot-steps in most flat rooms. A grown-up walks beside them and the floor is cleared first. The reflective strip step is optional, because not every home has one. The Words Only test needs only two people, paper and a clock. Sign Snap works for one child alone. The spine (intro, Kitchen Journey, Seen in the Dark, explanations, roots and quiz) fits about 85 minutes.

how_we_found_out.story: By the 1890s, scientists knew that radio waves travel in straight lines, like light. The Earth is round, so a straight line soon leaves the ground and heads off into space. Most experts therefore thought radio could never reach much beyond the horizon, perhaps a few hundred kilometres. Guglielmo Marconi, a young Italian inventor, tried anyway. In December 1901 he set up a receiver on a hill in Newfoundland, with its wire held up by a kite. He reported hearing three faint clicks, the letter S in Morse code, sent from Cornwall in England, about 3,400 kilometres away across the Atlantic. Some people doubted he really heard it. But within a few years his stations were sending messages across the ocean every day. In 1902, Arthur Kennelly and Oliver Heaviside suggested a reason: a layer of charged air high above the Earth that bends radio waves back down. In 1924, Edward Appleton and Miles Barnett proved it. They sent radio waves up from a BBC transmitter and timed the echoes coming back from this layer. Today we call it the ionosphere.
how_we_found_out.who: Guglielmo Marconi, Arthur Kennelly, Oliver Heaviside, Edward Appleton and Miles Barnett
how_we_found_out.when: 1901 (the signal across the Atlantic), 1902 (the idea of a reflecting layer), 1924 (Appleton and Barnett's proof)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Experts thought that because radio waves travel in straight lines, they could never follow the curve of the Earth to faraway places. Marconi's signal across the Atlantic showed that radio could go much further. The reason was a charged layer high in the air, the ionosphere, which sends some radio waves back down to the ground.
